item.title: The Rural Margin of Territorial Peace: Within-Municipality Evidence from Colombia
item.description: arXiv:2611.26882v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Colombia's peace agreement introduced participatory development programs and congressional constituencies reserved for conflict victims with a rural electorate. I use repeated waves of the Social Capital Barometer and a triple-difference event study to compare changes in rural-urban engagement gaps in municipalities covered by both reforms with those elsewhere. Rural engagement evolved more favorably relative to urban engagement in the covered municipalities. The index captures coordination around shared problems, civic participation and party linkage, with coordination providing the clearest evidence. The result persists when the reference period precedes the agreement and the baseline wave is excluded. Program activity and organizational membership patterns are consistent with participatory investment and political mobilization. The findings document a change in engagement beyond voting under the joint territorial reforms.
item.dc:creator: Hector Galindo-Silva

item.title: The Rise of Agents and the Human Labor Market
item.description: arXiv:2611.27210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We provide the first economy-wide and cross-AI model evidence on the effects of agentic AI on labor demand. We combine proprietary OpenRouter data covering about two quadrillion tokens of realized AI consumption (2 percent of global AI token consumption) across more than 400 AI models, including 1.1 quadrillion agentic tokens, with the full text of 34.8 million U.S. job postings for public firms from Lightcast. We compute our measure of firm-level exposure to aggregate agentic AI consumption (agentic beta) using the comovement of U.S. public firms' stock returns with realized weekly aggregate agentic AI token consumption. We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm's exposure to agentic AI predicts 2.11 percent lower growth in job postings over the next six months and 3.20 percent over nine months. We then conduct an event study based on the release of Claude Code 2.0, which significantly expanded the capabilities of AI agents, and show that a one-standard-deviation higher pre-release exposure to agentic AI predicts 4.73 percent lower posting growth over six months post the release. Furthermore, we show that the decrease in job postings is concentrated among non-senior jobs and is statistically insignificant for senior jobs. In contrast, we find no statistically significant relation between broad AI realized consumption exposure and subsequent job posting growth once agentic exposure is controlled for. Finally, we validate our market-implied agentic exposure measure using independent evidence from firms' mentions of AI deployment in securities filings and earnings calls.
item.dc:creator: Nicola Borri, Anton Cheremukhin, Yukun Liu, Aleh Tsyvinski

item.title: Trust and Lottery-Related Anomalies
item.description: arXiv:2611.27020v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We examine whether social trust shapes the pricing of lottery-like stocks by influencing investors' beliefs regarding optimistic information associated with extreme future payoffs. We argue that higher social trust reduces investors' skepticism toward optimistic information associated with extreme future payoffs, increasing demand for lottery-type stocks and leading to overpricing and lower subsequent returns. Using a sample of 8,875 firms across 49 US states over the period 1996-2018 and MAX as a proxy for lottery-like characteristics, we show that the MAX effect is concentrated in regions with relatively high trust and is weak or absent in regions with relatively low trust. We further find that this trust conditioning is stronger in regions with lower education or income levels, consistent with social trust playing a relatively more important role when investors have more limited access to private information. The results are robust to alternative lottery proxies and a range of robustness checks. Our findings identify social trust as a novel determinant of the pricing of lottery-like stocks and provide evidence that social capital may amplify belief-driven mispricing in assets with highly skewed payoffs.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Reza Bradrania, Ya Gao, Trust and Lottery-Related Anomalies, International Review of Economics & Finance, 2026, 106078

item.title: Keeping in Place After the Storm-Emergency Assistance and Evictions
item.description: arXiv:2505.14548v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We offer evidence that federal emergency assistance (FEMA) in the days following natural disasters mitigate evictions in comparison to similar emergency scenarios where FEMA aid is not provided. We find an approximate 10.9% increase in overall evictions after hurricane natural disaster events driven in large part by areas in close proximity of the hurricane path that do not receive FEMA rental assistance. Furthermore, we also show that FEMA aid acts as a liquidity buffer to other forms of emergency credit, specifically we find that overall transactions volumes decrease during hurricane events in locations that do receive FEMA aid. This effect largely reverses in areas that do not receive FEMA aid. Overall, this suggests that the availability of emergency liquidity during natural disaster events is indeed a binding constraint with real household financial consequences, in particular through our documented channel of evictions and in usage of high-cost credit.
item.dc:creator: Bilal Islah, Ahmed Zoulati

item.title: Advancing AI Capabilities and Evolving Labor Outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2507.08244v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper examines how labor market outcomes changed across occupations as AI capabilities advanced from chatbots to reasoning models and AI agents. We construct an occupational AI exposure score for each capability stage and relate its change to the Current Population Survey through June 2026. In aggregate, occupations whose exposure rose more did not lose employment or see higher unemployment over three years. However, the number of workers under 30 in these occupations fell by about 8 percent per standard deviation of the exposure change, and the decline is concentrated among young workers without a college degree and in office and customer service occupations rather than in technical occupations. Their unemployment did not rise, consistent with less entry rather than more layoffs. College graduates aged 30 to 49 gained full-time positions in the same occupations, so the workforce in exposed occupations became older and more educated. The same comparisons for 2017 to 2022 show no such patterns.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Dominski, Tyler Boes, Yong Suk Lee

item.title: Science under Threat? A Natural Experiment in Economics
item.description: arXiv:2608.14164v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Academic freedom is under strain worldwide. To study how scholars respond to (perceived) political pressure, we exploit a natural experiment in the United States: the publication in early 2025 of a "stop list" of words flagged by the government. We find that economists at universities relying more on federal funding reduce gender-, race-, and environment-related content with flagged words relative to other US and UK economists. Regarding mechanisms, our analyses suggest that self-censorship may explain this reduction better than direct grant cancellation. Estimates are similar when excluding papers acknowledging federal funding or controlling for universities' institutional measures and financial distress.
item.dc:creator: Dominic Rohner, Oliver Vanden Eynde, Philine Widmer

item.title: AI, Specialization, and the Organization of Knowledge Work: Evidence from Legal Services
item.description: arXiv:2611.23354v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Artificial intelligence makes specialized knowledge cheaper to use, but its effects on professional-service firms depend on how clients reallocate work and how suppliers respond. We develop a framework linking individual self-provision, enterprise make-or-buy decisions, and pricing by specialist firms. As AI improves lower-priced alternatives, clients may reallocate work across outside providers without bringing it in-house. If the departing work is more price-sensitive than the work that remains, premium firms may raise their optimal markups even as their share of work declines. We examine these margins in U.S. legal services. Across 89 federal districts, a difference-in-differences analysis finds a 6.6-percentage-point increase in non-prisoner self-representation relative to prisoner petitions by fiscal 2025, remaining substantial after adjusting for pre-existing trends. In contrast, lawyer employment shows no clear post-2022 shift toward client firms. Legal-AI benchmarks reveal continuing limitations in reliably completing complex, multi-step work, offering one possible explanation. Meanwhile, the largest law firms reported 13% revenue growth in 2025 despite nearly flat billable hours, while lower-priced firms experienced stronger demand growth. Reported AI integration is also stronger among firms with lower revenue per lawyer. These patterns highlight the importance of changes in work allocation and supplier competition, even as much of the underlying reallocation predates generative AI. The findings illustrate why cheaper expertise need not produce either widespread internalization or declining prices for premium professional services.
item.dc:creator: Liu Zhang, Mark Esposito, Isabel Yang

item.title: Rethinking Arrow--Debreu: A New Framework for Exchange
item.description: arXiv:2510.16003v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper revisits the Arrow--Debreu general equilibrium framework through the lens of effective trade, emphasizing the distinction between theoretical and realizable market interactions. We develop the Effective Trade Model (ETM), where transactions arise from bilateral feasibility rather than aggregate supply and demand desires. Within this framework, we establish the main properties of the price-demand correspondence and prove the existence of Nash equilibria, incorporating production, money, and network topology. Our results show that equilibrium is shaped by transaction constraints, subjective pricing, and decentralized negotiation, rather than by universal market-clearing conditions, and thereby call into question the foundations of welfare theory.
item.dc:creator: Nizar Riane
